arXiv:2410.21765v1 [math.AP] 29 Oct 2024

Stationary self-similar profiles for the two-dimensional inviscid Boussinesq equations

Ken Abe Ken AbeDepartment of Mathematics, Graduate School of Science, Osaka Metropolitan University, 3-3-138 Sugimoto, Sumiyoshi-ku Osaka, 558-8585, Japan Email address: kabe@omu.ac.jp , Daniel Ginsberg Daniel GinsbergDepartment of Mathematics, Brooklyn College (CUNY), Brooklyn, NY 11210, USA Email address: daniel.ginsberg@brooklyn.cuny.edu and In-Jee Jeong In-Jee JeongDepartment of Mathematical Sciences and RIM, Seoul National University, Seoul 08826, Korea Email address: injee_j@snu.ac.kr
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We consider (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions (stationary self-similar solutions of degree −α-\alpha) to the two-dimensional inviscid Boussinesq equations in a half-plane. We show their non-existence and existence with both regular and singular profile functions. More specifically, we demonstrate:

  • •

    Non-existence of rotational (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions with regular profiles
    (u,p,ρ)∈C1​(ℝ+2¯\{0})(u,p,\rho)\in C^{1}(\overline{\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+}}\backslash\{0\}) for 0≤α≤10\leq\alpha\leq 1 and (u,p,ρ)∈C2​(ℝ+2¯\{0})(u,p,\rho)\in C^{2}(\overline{\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+}}\backslash\{0\}) for −1/2≤α<0-1/2\leq\alpha<0

  • •

    Existence of rotational (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions with regular profiles
    (u,p,ρ)∈C2​(ℝ+2¯\{0})(u,p,\rho)\in C^{2}(\overline{\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+}}\backslash\{0\}) for α>1\alpha>1 and (u,p,ρ)∈C1​(ℝ+2¯)(u,p,\rho)\in C^{1}(\overline{\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+}}) for α<−2\alpha<-2

  • •

    Existence of rotational (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions with x1x_{1}-symmetric singular profiles
    (u,p,ρ)∈C∞(ℝ+2¯\{x1=0}∪{x2=0})∩C(ℝ+2¯)(u,p,\rho)\in C^{\infty}(\overline{\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+}}\backslash\{x_{1}=0\}\cup\{x_{2}=0\})\cap C(\overline{\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+}}) for −1<α<−1/2-1<\alpha<-1/2 and (u,p,ρ)∈C∞(ℝ+2¯\{x1=0}∪{x2=0})(u,p,\rho)\in C^{\infty}(\overline{\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+}}\backslash\{x_{1}=0\}\cup\{x_{2}=0\}) for −1/2≤α<1-1/2\leq\alpha<1

The (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions with continuous profiles (u,p,ρ)∈C∞(ℝ+2¯\{x1=0}∪{x2=0})∩C(ℝ+2¯)(u,p,\rho)\in C^{\infty}(\overline{\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+}}\backslash\{x_{1}=0\}\cup\{x_{2}=0\})\cap C(\overline{\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+}}) for −1<α<−1/2-1<\alpha<-1/2 provide examples to self-similar weak solutions in ℝ+2\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+} for the scaling exponent α≈−0.617\alpha\approx-0.617, at which Wang et al. (2023) numerically discovered the existence of backward self-similar solutions with smooth profile functions.

Key words and phrases: 
Self-similar solutions, Dubreil-Jacotin–Long equation, Minimax theorems, Singular elliptic problem

1. Introduction

The 2D inviscid Boussinesq equations

(1.1) ut+u⋅∇u+∇p\displaystyle u_{t}+u\cdot\nabla u+\nabla p =−ρ​e2,\displaystyle=-\rho e_{2},
∇⋅u\displaystyle\nabla\cdot u =0,\displaystyle=0,
ρt+u⋅∇ρ\displaystyle\rho_{t}+u\cdot\nabla\rho =0,\displaystyle=0,

describe the velocity u⁡(x,t)=(u1​(x,t),u2​(x,t))u(x,t)=(u^{1}(x,t),u^{2}(x,t)), the pressure p⁡(x,t)p(x,t), and the density ρ⁡(x,t)\rho(x,t) of stratified fluids when the density variation is small compared with the mean density. These equations can be derived from the equations of thermodynamics by the Boussinesq approximation [Obe79], [Obe88], [Bou03], incorporating the buoyancy force −ρ​e2-\rho e_{2} for e2=(0,1)e_{2}=(0,1) and are widely used to model stratified flows in geophysical fluid dynamics, e.g., [Val17, 2.4], [Dav13, Chapter 4], [DR82, Chapter 2], [Maj03]. The Boussinesq equations in a half-plane also share the essential structure of the axisymmetric Euler equations with swirl [MB02]. The problem of singularity formation for these two equations has attracted attention during the last decade; see Kiselev [Kis18] and Drivas and Elgindi [DE, 5.2] for surveys.

1.1. Self-similar solutions

We consider self-similar solutions to the Boussinesq equations (1.1). We say that (u,p,ρ)(u,p,\rho) is a backward (resp. forward) self-similar solution if

u⁡(x,t)=λα​u​(λ​x,λ1+α​t),p⁡(x,t)=λ2​α​u​(λ​x,λ1+α​t),ρ⁡(x,t)=λ2​α+1​ρ​(λ​x,λ1+α​t),\displaystyle u(x,t)=\lambda^{\alpha}u(\lambda x,\lambda^{1+\alpha}t),\quad p(x,t)=\lambda^{2\alpha}u(\lambda x,\lambda^{1+\alpha}t),\quad\rho(x,t)=\lambda^{2\alpha+1}\rho(\lambda x,\lambda^{1+\alpha}t),

for some α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R} and for all λ>0\lambda>0, x∈ℝ2x\in\mathbb{R}^{2} and t<0t<0 (resp. t>0t>0) [Cha07]. This self-similarity is of the second kind [ZR67], [Bar96], [EF09] in the sense that the scaling exponent α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R} is free in contrast to the viscous and diffusive Boussinesq equations where α=1\alpha=1 is dictated by the scaling of the problem (self-similarity of the first kind).

Self-similarity of the second kind plays an important role in the study of singularity formation in many equations of hydrodynamics:

  • •

    One-dimensional models: Various backward self-similar solutions have been discovered for the gCLM equations in the works of Elgindi and Jeong [EJ20b], Chen et al. [CHH21], Chen [Che20], Lushnikov et al. [LSS21], Huang et al. [HQWW24], [HQWW24], Zhen [Zhe23], and Jia and Šverák [Š]. They have the same scaling law as the inviscid Boussinesq equations and possess exponents distributing over the range α∈[−2,2]\alpha\in[-2,2]; see Table 1 in Appendix A.

  • •

    Shock formation: Backward self-similar solutions to the 1D inviscid Burgers equation with smooth profile functions exist for α=−1/(2i+1)\alpha=-1/(2i+1) and i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}, e.g., [EF09]. Higher dimensional anisotropic self-similar solutions for α=−1/3\alpha=-1/3 involving additional scaling exponents have been obtained in the work of Collot et al. [CGM22] in the study of the 2D Burgers equations with transverse viscosity and the work of Buckmaster et al. [BSV22] in the study of shock and singularity formation of the 3D isentropic compressible Euler equations, cf. [BSV23a], [BSV23b].

  • •

    Boundary layer separation: Collot et al. [CGM21] discovered two explicit backward self-similar solutions to the 2D inviscid Prandtl equations for α=−1/3\alpha=-1/3 with two different additional exponents modeling generic separation singularity relevant to Van-Dommelen–Shen boundary layer singularity and degenerate singularity relevant to Burgers shock; see [CGIM22] for a stability result in the Prandtl boundary layer equation.

  • •

    Implosions in compressible fluids: Merle et al. [MRRS22b] discovered backward self-similar solutions to the isentropic compressible Euler equations for exponents {αn}⊂(0,αo)\{\alpha_{n}\}\subset(0,\alpha_{\peye}) accumulating at the constant αo\alpha_{\peye} with smooth spherically symmetric profile functions slowly decaying at infinity. They describe blow-ups of isentropic compressible Navier–Stokes equations [MRRS22c] and supercritical defocusing nonlinear Schrödinger equations [MRRS22a]. Buckmaster et al. [BCLGSa] demonstrated that 33D imploding solutions exist for all adiabatic exponents γ>1\gamma>1; see [BCLGSb] for a review.

Returning to the Boussinseq equations (1.1), we distinguish the following four cases, cf. [CHH21, Definition 1.1], [DE, Definition 4.8, 4.1.10]:

Case 1: α=−1\alpha=-1 (Scale-invariant). The equation (1.1) is reduced to a system for 11-homogeneous velocity and density. Elgindi and Jeong [EJ20a] constructed finite energy blow-up solutions to the 2D inviscid Boussinesq equations in a corner domain by studying solutions of this type, cf. [DE, Problem 8]. See also Sarria and Wu [SW15] for infinite energy blow-up solutions in a strip.

Case 2: α>−1\alpha>-1 (Concentrating). (Time-dependent) backward self-similar solutions take the form

u⁡(x,t)=1(−t)αα+1​u​(x(−t)1α+1,−1),p⁡(x,t)=1(−t)2​αα+1​p​(x(−t)1α+1,−1),ρ⁡(x,t)=1(−t)2​α+1α+1​ρ​(x(−t)1α+1,−1),\displaystyle u(x,t)=\frac{1}{(-t)^{\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+1}}}u\left(\frac{x}{(-t)^{\frac{1}{\alpha+1}}},-1\right),\quad p(x,t)=\frac{1}{(-t)^{\frac{2\alpha}{\alpha+1}}}p\left(\frac{x}{(-t)^{\frac{1}{\alpha+1}}},-1\right),\quad\rho(x,t)=\frac{1}{(-t)^{\frac{2\alpha+1}{\alpha+1}}}\rho\left(\frac{x}{(-t)^{\frac{1}{\alpha+1}}},-1\right),

where the profile function (u,p,ρ)​(x,−1)(u,p,\rho)(x,-1) satisfies the self-similar equations:

(1.2) αα+1​u+1α+1​x⋅∇u+u⋅∇u+∇p\displaystyle\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+1}u+\frac{1}{\alpha+1}x\cdot\nabla u+u\cdot\nabla u+\nabla p =−ρ​e2,\displaystyle=-\rho e_{2},
∇⋅u\displaystyle\nabla\cdot u =0,\displaystyle=0,
2​α+1α+1​ρ+1α+1​x⋅∇ρ+u⋅∇ρ\displaystyle\frac{2\alpha+1}{\alpha+1}\rho+\frac{1}{\alpha+1}x\cdot\nabla\rho+u\cdot\nabla\rho =0.\displaystyle=0.

Elgindi [Elg21, Theorem 1 and Remark 1.3] provided the first example of backward self-similar solutions to the Euler equations in this class with some axisymmetric profile without swirl, and satisfying u⁡(x,−1)∈C1,γ​(ℝ3)u(x,-1)\in C^{1,\gamma}(\mathbb{R}^{3}) for small γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1). See also Elgindi et al. [EGM21] for a study of their stability. Chen and Hou [CH21] constructed asymptotically self-similar blow-up solutions to the 2D inviscid Boussinesq equations in a half-plane for some C1,γC^{1,\gamma} initial data. The recent works [CHa], [CHb] significantly extended the result for smooth initial data with a computer-assisted proof.

Case 3: α<−1\alpha<-1 (Expanding). Chen et al. [CHH21] discovered this type of backward self-similar solution for the De Gregorio model of the 3D Euler equations. See also Huang et al. [HTW23], cf. [Š]. They also exist for the generalized Constantin–Lax–Majda (gCLM) equations [HQWW24].

Case 4: α=∞\alpha=\infty (Separation of variables). Chen [Che21] found this type of self-similar solutions for the gCLM equations inspired by the numerical work of Lushnikov et al. [LSS21], cf. [HQWW24].

Wang et al. [WLGSB23] explored the existence of solutions to the backward self-similar equations (1.2) in a half-plane. The work [WLGSB23] numerically searched for smooth solutions satisfying the conditions ∇u\nabla u, ∇ρ→0\nabla\rho\to 0 as |x|→∞|x|\to\infty as well as the x1x_{1}-symmetry

(1.3) u1​(x1,x2)\displaystyle u^{1}(x_{1},x_{2}) =−u1(−x1,x2),u2(x1,x2)=u2(−x1,x2),\displaystyle=-u^{1}(-x_{1},x_{2}),\quad u^{2}(x_{1},x_{2})=u^{2}(-x_{1},x_{2}),
p⁡(x1,x2)\displaystyle p(x_{1},x_{2}) =p(−x1,x2),ρ(x1,x2)=ρ(−x1,x2),\displaystyle=p(-x_{1},x_{2}),\quad\rho(x_{1},x_{2})=\rho(-x_{1},x_{2}),

for unknown α>−1\alpha>-1 by using neural networks, and found solutions at the exponent α≈−0.617\alpha\approx-0.617 (in the notation of [WLGSB23, p.3], μ=−α/(α+1)≈1.917\mu=-\alpha/(\alpha+1)\approx 1.917). The work [WLGSB23] also found solutions to (1.2) peaked at the origin for the fixed exponent α=−0.75\alpha=-0.75 (μ=3\mu=3); see Figure 1.

In light of the above, it is natural to ask the following question:

Question 1.1.

For which exponents α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R} do self-similar solutions to the problem (1.1) exist?

1.2. The statement of the main results

1.2.1. Self-similar Boussinesq solutions

This work aims to answer Question 1.1 in the class of stationary solutions. We consider (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous (stationary self-similar) solutions of the form

u⁡(x)=1|x|α​u​(x|x|),p⁡(x)=1|x|2​α​p​(x|x|),ρ⁡(x)=1|x|2​α+1​ρ​(x|x|).\displaystyle u(x)=\frac{1}{|x|^{\alpha}}u\left(\frac{x}{|x|}\right),\quad p(x)=\frac{1}{|x|^{2\alpha}}p\left(\frac{x}{|x|}\right),\quad\rho(x)=\frac{1}{|x|^{2\alpha+1}}\rho\left(\frac{x}{|x|}\right).

The (−α)(-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions to (1.1) are also solutions to the self-similar equations (1.2). We identify solutions of (1.1) in a half-plane with those in the whole plane under the x2x_{2}-symmetry:

(1.4) u1​(x1,x2)\displaystyle u^{1}(x_{1},x_{2}) =u1(x1,−x2),u2(x1,x2)=−u2(x1,−x2),\displaystyle=u^{1}(x_{1},-x_{2}),\quad u^{2}(x_{1},x_{2})=-u^{2}(x_{1},-x_{2}),
p⁡(x1,x2)\displaystyle p(x_{1},x_{2}) =p(x1,−x2),ρ(x1,x2)=−ρ(x1,−x2).\displaystyle=p(x_{1},-x_{2}),\quad\rho(x_{1},x_{2})=-\rho(x_{1},-x_{2}).

We say that (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions (u,p,ρ)(u,p,\rho) have regular profiles if (u,p,ρ)(u,p,\rho) is a classical stationary solution to (1.1) in ℝ2\{0}\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}. Otherwise, we say that (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions (u,p,ρ)(u,p,\rho) have singular profiles. First, we state one of the main results about the non-existence and existence of rotational (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions with regular profiles. We give a concrete characterization of irrotational (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions with regular profiles in Theorem 1.9.

Theorem 1.2 (Rotational solutions with regular profiles).

The following holds for rotational (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions to (1.1) and (1.4):

(i) For 0≤α≤10\leq\alpha\leq 1, no solutions (u,p,ρ)∈C1​(ℝ2\{0})(u,p,\rho)\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}) exist.
(ii) For −1/2≤α<0-1/2\leq\alpha<0, no solutions (u,p,ρ)∈C2​(ℝ2\{0})(u,p,\rho)\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}) exist.
(iii) For α>1\alpha>1, solutions (u,p,ρ)∈C2​(ℝ2\{0})(u,p,\rho)\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}) exist.
(iv) For α<−2\alpha<-2, solutions (u,p,ρ)∈C1​(ℝ2)(u,p,\rho)\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) exist.

Figure 1 (A) shows the non-existence and existence ranges of α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R} for rotational (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions with regular profiles. The main result of this paper is the existence of (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions to (1.1) with singular profiles for −1<α<1-1<\alpha<1 satisfying the x1x_{1}-symmetry (1.3). They provide examples of stationary self-similar weak solutions for α≈−0.617\alpha\approx-0.617, at which Wang et al. [WLGSB23] numerically discovered the existence of backward self-similar solutions to (1.1) with smooth profile functions.

Theorem 1.3 (Rotational solutions with singular profiles).

The following holds for rotational (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions to (1.1), (1.3), and (1.4):

(i) For −1<α<−1/2-1<\alpha<-1/2, solutions (u,p,ρ)∈C∞(ℝ2\{x1=0}∪{x2=0})∩C(ℝ2)(u,p,\rho)\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{x_{1}=0\}\cup\{x_{2}=0\})\cap C(\mathbb{R}^{2}) exist.
(ii) For −1/2≤α<1-1/2\leq\alpha<1, solutions (u,p,ρ)∈C∞(ℝ2\{x1=0}∪{x2=0})(u,p,\rho)\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{x_{1}=0\}\cup\{x_{2}=0\}) exist.

The solutions in (i) are weak solutions to (1.1) in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} and the C1C^{1}-norm of uu diverges on the axis {x1=0}\{x_{1}=0\}. The velocity uu is (−α-\alpha)-Hölder continuous for the radial variable and (2+2/(α−1)2+2/(\alpha-1))-Hölder continuous for the angular variable. The solutions in (ii) satisfy (1.1) in ℝ2\{x1=0}∪{x2=0}\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{x_{1}=0\}\cup\{x_{2}=0\} and the C1C^{1}-norm of uu diverges on the axis {x1=0}\{x_{1}=0\}.

Remark 1.4 (−1<α<−1/2-1<\alpha<-1/2).

The non-existence and existence of rotational (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions for −1<α<−1/2-1<\alpha<-1/2 with regular profiles are generally unknown; see Theorems 1.5 and 1.7. We remark that the profile of backward self-similar solutions to the axisymmetric Euler equations without swirl [Elg21] are regular and belong to C1,γC^{1,\gamma} for small γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1).

1.2.2. Self-similar Euler solutions

In the sequel, we consider two particular stationary solutions to (1.1): the 2D Euler solutions ρ≡0\rho\equiv 0 and constant Bernoulli function solutions Π=p+|u|2/2+x2​ρ≡const.\Pi=p+|u|^{2}/2+x_{2}\rho\equiv\textrm{const.} (Pseudo-Beltrami solutions).

Elling [Ell16] constructed forward self-similar weak solutions to the 2D Euler equations in the whole plane for −1<α<1/2-1<\alpha<1/2 and (−α−1-\alpha-1)-homogeneous initial vorticity ω0​(x)=|x|−α−1​ω0​(x/|x|)\omega_{0}(x)=|x|^{-\alpha-1}\omega_{0}(x/|x|) with 2​π/m2\pi/m-periodic ω0\omega_{0} in the Wiener algebra ω0​(ϕ)∈A⁡(𝕊1)⊂C⁡(𝕊1)\omega_{0}(\phi)\in A(\mathbb{S}^{1})\subset C(\mathbb{S}^{1}) for arbitrary m≥m0m\geq m_{0} for some m0∈ℕm_{0}\in\mathbb{N}. Here, ω=∇⟂⋅u\omega=\nabla^{\perp}\cdot u and ∇⟂=(−∂2,∂1)\nabla^{\perp}=(-\partial_{2},\partial_{1}). Shao et al. [SWZ] extended the result to −1<α<1-1<\alpha<1 and 2​π/m2\pi/m-periodic ω0∈L1​(𝕊1)\omega_{0}\in L^{1}(\mathbb{S}^{1}) for arbitrary m≥2m\geq 2 (and also for measures ω0∈ℳ⁡(𝕊1)\omega_{0}\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{S}^{1})) (The self-similar equations to forward self-similar solutions are the equations (1.2) replacing the signs of the first two terms in (1.2)1(1.2)_{1} and (1.2)3(1.2)_{3} by minus). Jeong [Jeo17] and Elgindi and Jeong [EJ20c] constructed unique scale-invariant weak solutions (α=−1\alpha=-1) for bounded 00-homogeneous mm-fold symmetric initial vorticity for m≥3m\geq 3; see also Elgindi et al. [EMS] and Jeong and Said [JS] for long-time behavior.

García and Gómez-Serrano [GGS] constructed forward self-similar weak solutions to the generalized surface quasi-geostrophic (gSQG) equations for γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1) and 1<α<1+γ1<\alpha<1+\gamma for 2​π/m2\pi/m-periodic ω0∈Lp​(𝕊1)\omega_{0}\in L^{p}(\mathbb{S}^{1}) for p>1/(1−γ)p>1/(1-\gamma) (The cases γ=0\gamma=0 and γ=1\gamma=1 correspond to the Euler equations and the SQG equations, respectively; see Figure 2 (A)).

Theorems 1.5 and 1.6 show the non-existence and existence of rotational (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous 2D Euler solutions with regular profiles and the existence of rotational (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous 2D Euler solutions with singular profiles, respectively. Theorem 1.6 is essentially due to the recent work of Elgindi and Huang [EH, Lemma 5.3]. This statement includes the case 0<α<10<\alpha<1 and detailed properties of profile functions. Theorem 1.5 is due to [Abe24, Theorem 1.7]. It turns out that the non-existence range of (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions with regular profiles agrees with the existence range of (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions with singular profiles in this class; see Figure 2 (B) and (C).

Theorem 1.5 (2D Euler solutions with regular profiles).

The following holds for rotational (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions to (1.1) and (1.4) for ρ≡0\rho\equiv 0:

(i) For 0≤α≤10\leq\alpha\leq 1, no solutions (u,p)∈C1​(ℝ2\{0})(u,p)\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}) exist.
(ii) For −1≤α<0-1\leq\alpha<0, no solutions (u,p)∈C2​(ℝ2\{0})(u,p)\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}) exist.
(iii) For α>1\alpha>1, solutions (u,p)∈C2​(ℝ2\{0})(u,p)\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}) exist.
(iv) For α<−1\alpha<-1, solutions (u,p)∈C1​(ℝ2)(u,p)\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) exist.

Theorem 1.6 (2D Euler solutions with singular profiles).

The following holds for rotational (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions to (1.1), (1.3), and (1.4) for ρ≡0\rho\equiv 0:

(i) For −1<α<0-1<\alpha<0, solutions (u,p)∈C∞(ℝ2\{x1=0}∪{x2=0})∩C(ℝ2)(u,p)\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{x_{1}=0\}\cup\{x_{2}=0\})\cap C(\mathbb{R}^{2}) exist.
(ii) For 0<α<10<\alpha<1, solutions (u,p)∈C∞(ℝ2\{x1=0}∪{x2=0})(u,p)\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{x_{1}=0\}\cup\{x_{2}=0\}) exist.

The solutions in (i) are weak solutions to (1.1) in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} and the C1C^{1}-norm of uu diverges on the axis {x1=0}∪{x2=0}\{x_{1}=0\}\cup\{x_{2}=0\}. The velocity uu is (−α-\alpha)-Hölder continuous for the radial variable and (2+2/(α−1)2+2/(\alpha-1))-Hölder continuous for the angular variable. The solutions in (ii) satisfy (1.1) in ℝ2\{x1=0}∪{x2=0}\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{x_{1}=0\}\cup\{x_{2}=0\}. The velocity uu diverges on the axis {x1=0}∪{x2=0}\{x_{1}=0\}\cup\{x_{2}=0\}.

1.2.3. Self-similar Pseudo-Beltrami solutions

The other class of stationary solutions to (1.1) are solutions with constant Bernoulli function Π=p+|u|2/2+x2​ρ\Pi=p+|u|^{2}/2+x_{2}\rho. We show that this class excludes (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions with regular profiles for −2<α<−1-2<\alpha<-1 in contrast to the 2D Euler case in Theorem 1.5 (iv), cf. Remark 1.4. On the other hand, the existence range of (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions with singular profiles is restricted to −1<α<1-1<\alpha<1.

Theorem 1.7 (Pseudo-Beltrami solutions with regular profiles).

The following holds for rotational (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions to (1.1) and (1.3) for Π≡const.\Pi\equiv\textrm{const.}:

(i) For −1/2≤α≤1-1/2\leq\alpha\leq 1, no solutions (u,p,ρ)∈C1​(ℝ2\{0})(u,p,\rho)\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}) exist.
(ii) For −2<α<−1/2-2<\alpha<-1/2, no solutions (u,p,ρ)∈C2​(ℝ2\{0})(u,p,\rho)\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}) exist. For α=−2\alpha=-2, no solutions (u,p,ρ)∈C2​(ℝ2\{0})(u,p,\rho)\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}) exist provided that ∇⟂⋅u/x2\nabla^{\perp}\cdot u/x_{2} vanishes on x2=0x_{2}=0.
(iii) For α>1\alpha>1, solutions (u,p,ρ)∈C2​(ℝ2\{0})(u,p,\rho)\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}) exist.
(iv) For α<−2\alpha<-2, solutions (u,p,ρ)∈C1​(ℝ2)(u,p,\rho)\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) exist.

Theorem 1.8 (Pseudo-Beltrami solutions with singular profiles).

The following holds for rotational (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions to (1.1), (1.3), and (1.4) for Π≡const.\Pi\equiv\textrm{const.}:

(i) For −1<α<−1/2-1<\alpha<-1/2, solutions (u,p,ρ)∈C∞(ℝ2\{x1=0}∪{x2=0})∩C(ℝ2)(u,p,\rho)\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{x_{1}=0\}\cup\{x_{2}=0\})\cap C(\mathbb{R}^{2}) exist.
(ii) For −1/2<α<1-1/2<\alpha<1, solutions (u,p,ρ)∈C∞(ℝ2\{x1=0}∪{x2=0})(u,p,\rho)\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{x_{1}=0\}\cup\{x_{2}=0\}) exist.

The solutions in (i) and (ii) have the same properties as those in Theorem 1.3.

1.2.4. Self-similar irrotational solutions

We completely classify irrotational (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions to (1.1). Their velocity fields are harmonic vector fields u≠0u\neq 0 for integers α∈ℤ\alpha\in\mathbb{Z} or u=0u=0 with x2x_{2}-dependent functions p=p⁡(x2)p=p(x_{2}) and ρ=ρ⁡(x2)\rho=\rho(x_{2}) (static equilibria). We use polar coordinates (r,ϕ)(r,\phi) and the orthogonal frame er=(cos⁡ϕ,sin⁡ϕ)e_{r}=(\cos\phi,\sin\phi) and eϕ=(−sin⁡ϕ,cos⁡ϕ)e_{\phi}=(-\sin\phi,\cos\phi).

Irrotational (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions (u,p,ρ)∈C1​(ℝ2\{0})(u,p,\rho)\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}) to (1.1) and (1.4) are either the following (i) or (ii):
(i) The velocity field is the harmonic vector field

If ρ≡0\rho\equiv 0, α=0\alpha=0 and the pressure pp is constant. If ρ≢0\rho\nequiv 0, α<−1\alpha<-1.

1.2.5. Desingularization of self-similar vortex sheets

We finally show the convergence of (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions of (1.1) with regular profiles to the (−1-1)-homogeneous vortex sheet solution with singular profiles as α→1+0\alpha\to 1+0. This convergence issue appears in current sheet formation in astrophysics [LBB94], [Aly94]. All (−1-1)-homogeneous solutions to (1.1) with regular profiles are the irrotational solution (1.5) by Theorems 1.2 (i) and 1.9. The (−1)(-1)-homogeneous irrotational solution for C=−1/2C=-1/2 and b=−1/8b=-1/8 in (1.5) take the form

(1.8) uir​(x)=12​r​er,pir​(x)=−18​r2.\displaystyle u_{\textrm{ir}}(x)=\frac{1}{2r}e_{r},\qquad p_{\textrm{ir}}(x)=-\frac{1}{8r^{2}}.

See Figure 4 (A) for streamlines.

Rotational (−1-1)-homogeneous solutions with singular profiles can be constructed by replacing ere_{r} by −er-e_{r} on intervals in [0,π][0,\pi]. The simplest one forms

(1.9) ush​(x)={−12​r​er0<ϕ<π2,12​r​erπ2<ϕ<π.psh​(x)=−18​r2.\displaystyle u_{\textrm{sh}}(x)=\begin{cases}\ -\displaystyle\frac{1}{2r}e_{r}\quad&0<\phi<\displaystyle\frac{\pi}{2},\\ \ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2r}e_{r}\quad&\displaystyle\frac{\pi}{2}<\phi<\pi.\end{cases}\qquad p_{\textrm{sh}}(x)=-\frac{1}{8r^{2}}.

The solution (1.9) is a weak solution to the 2D Euler equations in ℝ2\{0}\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\} satisfying the x2x_{2}-symmetry (1.4) with the discontinuous velocity field ush∈C1(ℝ2\{x1=0})u_{\textrm{sh}}\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{x_{1}=0\}) producing the vortex sheet ωsh=r−2​δπ/2​(ϕ)\omega_{\textrm{sh}}=r^{-2}\delta_{\pi/2}(\phi), cf. [MB02, Chapter 9]. See Figure 4 (B) for streamlines. Self-similar vortex sheet solutions are relevant to non-uniqueness and long-time behavior of solutions to the 2D Euler equations; see Elling and Gnann [EG19], Cieślak et al. [CKO24b], [CKO22], [CKO24a], Jeong and Said [JS], and Shao et al. [SWZ]. We show that (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions to the Boussinesq equations desingularize the (−1-1)-homogeneous vortex sheet solution (1.9); see Figure 4 (C).

Theorem 1.10 (Desingularization as α→1+0\alpha\to 1+0).

There exist (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions (uα,pα,ρα)∈C2​(ℝ2\{0})(u_{\alpha},p_{\alpha},\rho_{\alpha})\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash\{0\}) to (1.1) and (1.4) for 1<α<21<\alpha<2 such that rα​uα→r​ushr^{\alpha}u_{\alpha}\to ru_{\textrm{sh}}, r2​α​pα→r2​pshr^{2\alpha}p_{\alpha}\to r^{2}p_{\textrm{sh}}, and r2​α+1​ρα→0r^{2\alpha+1}\rho_{\alpha}\to 0 locally uniformly for ϕ∈𝕊1\{±π/2}\phi\in\mathbb{S}^{1}\backslash\{\pm\pi/2\} as α→1+0\alpha\to 1+0. The function r2​α​pαr^{2\alpha}p_{\alpha} converges to r2​pshr^{2}p_{\textrm{sh}} also at ϕ=±π/2\phi=\pm\pi/2.

This study’s (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions provide examples of singular stationary solutions belonging to supercritical spaces for the local well-posedness of the 2D inviscid Boussinesq equations. These examples may reveal interesting behavior of nonstationary solutions in supercritical regimes; see, e.g., works on the 2D Euler equations: loss of regularity in time [Jeo21], [CMZO] and non-uniqueness [Ell16], [Visa], [Visb], [EH], [SWZ].

1.3. Relevant works on stratified flows: blow-up and stability

1.3.1. The singularity formation

The singularity formation of the 2D inviscid Boussinesq equations has attracted attention during the last decade. Chae [Cha07, Theorem 2.4] investigated the non-existence of backward self-similar solutions to the 2D inviscid Boussinesq equations. Chae and Wolf [CW19] and Chae and Constantin [CC21] established non-blow-up criteria that exclude self-similar singularities for solutions to the inviscid Boussinesq equations.

Elgindi and Jeong [EJ20a] constructed scale-invariant blow-up solutions (α=−1\alpha=-1) to the inviscid Boussinesq equations in a corner domain of angle π/2\pi/2. It is an open question [DE, Problem 8] whether scale-invariant solutions with vanishing vorticity and density gradient on the boundary exist. Elgindi and Pasqualotto [EPa], [EPb] constructed blow-up solutions in the whole plane for some C1,γC^{1,\gamma} initial data smooth except for the origin. Córdoba et al. [CMZZ] and Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa [CMZ] discussed non-self-similar and non-axisymmetric blow-up solutions to the Euler equations; see also Chen [Che].

1.3.2. Stability of static equilibrium

The static equilibrium p=p⁡(x2)p=p(x_{2}) and ρ⁡(x2)=p′​(x2)\rho(x_{2})=p^{\prime}(x_{2}) is a physically important steady-state of the inviscid Boussinesq equations describing a stable density of lighter fluid above and heavier fluid below. Elgindi and Widmayer [EW15] and Jurja and Widmayer [JW] show the local in-time stability of the 11-homogeneous static equilibrium

(1.10) us=0,ps=12​x22,ρs=−x2.\displaystyle u_{s}=0,\quad p_{s}=\frac{1}{2}x_{2}^{2},\quad\rho_{s}=-x_{2}.

Elgindi [Elg17], Castro et al. [CCL19a], and Bianchini et al. [BCBP23] demonstrated the asymptotic stability of the 11-homogeneous static equilibrium in the IPM equation. See also Castro et al. [CCL19b] and Tao et al. [TWZZ20] for stability in other systems. Kiselev and Yao [KY23] and Kiselev et al. [KPY] demonstrated density gradient growth (small-scale formations) both in the IPM equations and in the 2D inviscid Boussinesq equations. The work [KY23] showed the instability of the 11-homogeneous static equilibrium in the IPM equations with low regular norms, cf. [CCL19a]. See also Bianchini et al. [BCMZ] for the ill-posedness result to the IPM equations in H2H^{2}, cf. [CGO07].

Masmoudi et al. [MSHZ22] demonstrated the asymptotic stability of the static equilibria with Couette flow in the viscous Boussinesq equations without diffusivity. Bedrossian et al. [BBCZD23] showed the stability of static equilibria with Couette flow in the inviscid Boussinesq equations and vorticity and density gradient growth during the existence of smooth solutions (shear-buoyancy instability).

1.4. Ideas of the proof

We demonstrate the main theorems of this paper in the following order:

  • (I)

    The non-existence of (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions with regular profiles

  • (II)

    The existence of (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions with regular profiles

  • (III)

    The existence of (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions with singular profiles

The approaches to (I) and (II) are based on works on homogeneous solutions to the 3D Euler equations [LS15], [Shv18], and [Abe24]; see [BV22, 6.1.2]. We consider the stationary analog between the axisymmetric Euler equations and the 2D inviscid Boussinesq equations. The approach to (I) is based on the homogeneous Boussinesq equations on the semi-circle. The approach to (II) is based on the Dubreil-Jacotin–Long equation for the stream function [DJ35], [Lon53], cf. [Yih58], [Yih65, Chapter 3], [CLV19], [CDG21]. We consider the 1D homogeneous Dubreil-Jacotin–Long equation for the angular variable ϕ∈[0,π]\phi\in[0,\pi] with positive nonlinear powers and construct (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions with regular profiles by applying three minimax theorems according to α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R} values.

The completely new part of this study is (III) the existence of homogeneous solutions with singular profiles. We construct solutions to the 1D homogeneous Dubreil-Jacotin–Long equation with negative nonlinear powers. This equation is non-autonomous and not integrable, unlike the case of the 2D Euler equations [EH]. We construct solutions to the non-autonomous equation based on the maximum principle [dP92].

We outline the approaches to (I)–(III).

1.4.1. The non-existence of homogeneous solutions with regular profiles

The (−α)(-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions u=r−α​(a⁡(ϕ)​eϕ+f⁡(ϕ)​er)u=r^{-\alpha}(a(\phi)e_{\phi}+f(\phi)e_{r}), p=r−2​α​p​(ϕ)p=r^{-2\alpha}p(\phi), and ρ=r−2​α−1​ρ​(ϕ)\rho=r^{-2\alpha-1}\rho(\phi) to (1.1) and (1.4) satisfy the equations on the semi-circle:

1.4.2. The existence of homogeneous solutions with regular profiles

The main contribution of this work is the existence of homogeneous solutions to (1.1) and (1.4). The density ρ\rho and the Bernoulli function Π\Pi are the first integrals of the velocity field u=∇⟂ψu=\nabla^{\perp}\psi and locally are functions of the stream function ψ\psi. We assume that they are global functions of ψ\psi in a half-plane, i.e., Π=Π⁡(ψ)\Pi=\Pi(\psi) and ρ=ρ⁡(ψ)\rho=\rho(\psi). Then, the momentum equation u⟂ω+∇Π=x2∇ρu^{\perp}\omega+\nabla\Pi=x_{2}\nabla\rho for the π/2\pi/2 counter-clockwise rotation of the velocity u⟂=(−u2,u1)u^{\perp}=(-u^{2},u^{1}) implies that the stream function is a solution to the Dubreil-Jacotin–Long equation [DJ35], [Lon53], cf.     1≤β1\leq\beta: Linking theorem

    β<−2\beta<-2: Saddle point theorem

The main steps of applying those minimax theorems are to verify the Palais–Smale conditions for the functional II and to obtain inequalities of the form infNI>maxM0⁡I\inf_{N}I>\max_{M_{0}}I for suitable subsets NN and M0M_{0} in H01​(0,π)H^{1}_{0}(0,\pi). We show the Palais–Smale conditions for the superlinear case β>0\beta>0 and for the sublinear case β<−2\beta<-2 respectively, and choose suitable subsets NN and M0M_{0} in H01​(0,π)H^{1}_{0}(0,\pi) according to the values of β\beta to obtain the inequality infNI>maxM0⁡I\inf_{N}I>\max_{M_{0}}I.

For 0<β<10<\beta<1, a mountain pass theorem applied to a modified functional to (1.23) and a strong maximum principle imply the existence of positive and even symmetric solutions to (1.20) for ϕ=π/2\phi=\pi/2 in (0,π)(0,\pi).

The existence of solutions to (1.20) for (β,c1,c2)(\beta,c_{1},c_{2}) satisfying (1.22) implies (iii) and (iv) of Theorems 1.2, 1.5, and 1.7.

1.4.3. The existence of homogeneous solutions with singular profiles

The main results in this work (Theorems 1.3, 1.6, and 1.8) are based on the existence of solutions to the homogeneous Dubreil-Jacotin–Long equation (1.20) with negative nonlinear powers for (β,c1,c2)(\beta,c_{1},c_{2}) satisfying

1.5. Organization of the paper

Section 2 demonstrates the rigidity of (−α)(-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions (Theorem 1.9 and (i) and (ii) of Theorems 1.2, 1.5, and 1.7). Section 3 shows the existence of (−α)(-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions with regular profiles ((iii) and (iv) of Theorems 1.2, 1.5, and 1.7). Section 4 shows the existence of (−α)(-\alpha)-homogeneous solutions with singular profiles (Theorems 1.3, 1.6, and 1.8). Section 5 demonstrates the desingularization of the (−1-1)-homogeneous vortex sheet solution (Theorem 1.10). Appendix A reviews the existence of backward self-similar solutions to quasi-linear fluid equations.

Lemma 2.3.

Let −1≤α≤1-1\leq\alpha\leq 1. Let (u,p)(u,p) be a (−α-\alpha)-homogeneous solution to (1.1) and (1.4) for ρ≡0\rho\equiv 0. Assume that

3.3. The three minimax theorems

According to [Wil96], we define the Palais–Smale condition and state three minimax theorems for a Banach space XX equipped with the norm ||⋅||X||\cdot||_{X}. Let C1​(X,ℝ)C^{1}(X;\mathbb{R}) be the space of all functionals I⁡[⋅]:X→ℝI[\cdot]:X\to\mathbb{R} such that the Fréchet derivative I′:X→X∗I^{\prime}:X\to X^{*} exists and is continuous on XX. We say that w∈Xw\in X is a critical point of II if

⟨I′​[w],η⟩=0for all​η∈X.\displaystyle\langle I^{\prime}[w],\eta\rangle=0\quad\textrm{for all}\ \eta\in X.

The constant c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R} is a critical value if a critical point w∈Xw\in X exists, such as c=I⁡[w]c=I[w].

Definition 3.5 (Palais–Smale condition).

We say that a sequence {wn}⊂X\{w_{n}\}\subset X is a Palais–Smale sequence at level c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R} if

I⁡[wn]\displaystyle I[w_{n}] →c,\displaystyle\to c,
I′​[wn]\displaystyle I^{\prime}[w_{n}] →0inX∗.\displaystyle\to 0\quad\textrm{in}\ X^{*}.

We say that II satisfies the (PS)c(\textrm{PS})_{c} condition if any Palais–Smale sequence at level c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R} has a convergent subsequence in XX.

The following three minimax theorems are due to Ambrosetti and Rabinowitz [Wil96, Theorems 2.10, 2.11, 2.12].

Lemma 3.6 (Mountain pass theorem).

Assume that there exist w0∈Xw_{0}\in X and r0>0r_{0}>0 such that ‖w0‖X>r0||w_{0}||_{X}>r_{0} and

inf‖w‖X=r0I⁡[w]>I⁡[0]≥I⁡[w0].\displaystyle\inf_{||w||_{X}=r_{0}}I[w]>I[0]\geq I[w_{0}].

c\displaystyle c =infγ∈Λmax0≤t≤1⁡I⁡[γ⁡(t)],\displaystyle=\inf_{\gamma\in\Lambda}\max_{0\leq t\leq 1}I[\gamma(t)],
Λ\displaystyle\Lambda ={γ∈C([0,1];X)|γ(0)=0,γ(1)=w0}.\displaystyle=\left\{\gamma\in C([0,1];X)\ \middle|\ \gamma(0)=0,\ \gamma(1)=w_{0}\ \right\}.

Then, cc is a critical value of II.

3.6. The Palais–Smale condition

We show that the functional II satisfies the Palais–Smale condition. The primary step of the proof is to obtain the boundedness of the Palais–Smale sequence for the superlinear case β>0\beta>0 and for the sublinear case β<−2\beta<-2.

For 0<β<10<\beta<1, the Palais–Smale sequence is bounded by the identity (3.25) and the coercive estimate (3.22) on H01​(D)H^{1}_{0}(D). For β≥1\beta\geq 1, we use the direct sum decomposition (3.11) with the finite-dimensional space YY and the coercive estimate (3.23) on ZZ. By a contradiction argument, we show the boundedness of the Palais–Smale sequence for all β>0\beta>0.

Remark 4.14 (Singular elliptic problems).

The above problem is the one-dimensional analog of the singular elliptic problem

(4.19) −Δ​ψ\displaystyle-\Delta\psi =k(x)ψ−νinΩ,\displaystyle=k(x)\psi^{-\nu}\quad\textrm{in}\ \Omega,
ψ\displaystyle\psi =0on∂Ω,\displaystyle=0\quad\textrm{on}\ \partial\Omega,

for a non-negative function kk in a bounded domain Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}, n≥2n\geq 2 with constant ν>0\nu>0; see [FM60], [Stu], and [CRT77] for the origin of the problem (4.19). For positive k⁡(x)>0k(x)>0 in Ω¯\overline{\Omega}, ν=1\nu=1 is the threshold for C1C^{1} regularity on the boundary. For ν>1\nu>1, ψ∉C1​(Ω¯)\psi\notin C^{1}(\overline{\Omega}) and ψ∈C2/(ν+1)​(Ω¯)\psi\in C^{2/(\nu+1)}(\overline{\Omega}) [LM91]. For functions k⁡(x)k(x) vanishing on the boundary, the regularity of solutions has been investigated in [dP92], [GL93] under the condition, e.g., k⁡(x)≈dist​(x,∂Ω)k(x)\approx\textrm{dist}(x,\partial\Omega), cf. [FQS12, Theorem 8]. The C1C^{1}-threshold for such kk is ν=2\nu=2 and for ν>2\nu>2, ψ∉C1​(Ω¯)\psi\notin C^{1}(\overline{\Omega}) and ψ∈C3/(ν+1)​(Ω¯)\psi\in C^{3/(\nu+1)}(\overline{\Omega}). See [OP] for a survey and also [FQS12], [BG19] for recent works on singular problems of fully nonlinear equations.

The singular 1D problem (4.7) is similar to the classical problem (4.19), though the fact that the function k⁡(ϕ)=sin⁡ϕk(\phi)=\sin\phi vanishes only at one side of the boundary ϕ=0\phi=0 leads to different regularity at ϕ=0\phi=0 and π/2\pi/2.

The identity

|w′|2+β2​w2+2​c11−s​w1−s+2​c21−s′​sin⁡ϕ​w1−s′+2​c21−s′​∫ϕπ/4cos⁡ϕ~​w1−s′​d​ϕ~=C,ϕ∈D,\displaystyle|w^{\prime}|^{2}+\beta^{2}w^{2}+\frac{2c_{1}}{1-s}w^{1-s}+\frac{2c_{2}}{1-s^{\prime}}\sin\phi w^{1-s^{\prime}}+\frac{2c_{2}}{1-s^{\prime}}\int_{\phi}^{\pi/4}\cos\tilde{\phi}w^{1-s^{\prime}}\textrm{d}\tilde{\phi}=C,\quad\phi\in D,

holds for solutions to (4.7) with some constant CC by multiplying 2​w′2w^{\prime} by (4.7) and integrating it on (π/4,ϕ)(\pi/4,\phi). For −1<β<0-1<\beta<0, 1<s<s′1<s<s^{\prime} and w′w^{\prime} diverges on the boundary ϕ=0\phi=0 and π/2\pi/2. For −2<β<−3/2-2<\beta<-3/2, s<s′<1s<s^{\prime}<1 and w∈C1​(D¯)w\in C^{1}(\overline{D}). Moreover, w′∈C2+2/β​(D¯)w^{\prime}\in C^{2+2/\beta}(\overline{D}).

Appendix A The second kind self-similarities in hydrodynamics

We review existence results on backward self-similar solutions to the following fluid equations:

  • •

    gCLM equations

  • •

    Burgers equation

  • •

    Prandtl equations

  • •

    Isentropic compressible Euler equations

Those equations partially share the essential features with the 2D inviscid Boussinesq equations in a half-plane, such as advection and stretching of vorticity, incompressible flows in a half-plane, density variation, etc., and possess similar scaling laws; see Table 1.

A.1. One-dimensional vortex singularities

A canonical 1D blow-up model for the 3D Euler equations is the gCLM equations

(A.1) ωt+a​u​ωx=ω​ux,ux=H​ω,x∈ℝ.\omega_{t}+au\omega_{x}=\omega u_{x},\quad u_{x}=H\omega,\quad x\in\mathbb{R}.

Constantin et al. [CLM85] introduced this equation for a=0a=0 as a 1D model for vorticity of the 3D Euler equations incorporating the vortex stretching and the Biot–Savart law with the Hilbert transform HH and demonstrated that the equation exhibits a blow-up. Later, De Gregorio [DG90] added the advection term a=1a=1, and the continuum model for 0≤a≤10\leq a\leq 1 is due to Okamoto et al. [OSW08]. See also Córdoba et al. [CCF05] and Castro and Córdoba [CC10] for the case a=−1a=-1. The self-similar equations of the gCLM equations form

ω+1α+1​x​ωx+a​u​ωx=ω​ux,ux=H​ω,x∈ℝ.\displaystyle\omega+\frac{1}{\alpha+1}x\omega_{x}+au\omega_{x}=\omega u_{x},\quad u_{x}=H\omega,\quad x\in\mathbb{R}.

Elgindi and Jeong [EJ20b, 1.5, Proposition 2.1] found the explicit solution to the CLM equations (a=0a=0) with the scaling exponent α=0\alpha=0:

ω⁡(x)=x1+x2,u⁡(x)=−arctan⁡x.\displaystyle\omega(x)=\frac{x}{1+x^{2}},\quad u(x)=-\arctan{x}.

The work [EJ20b] demonstrated the existence of smooth profile functions ω∈C∞\omega\in C^{\infty} for small |a||a| with some exponent α∈(−1,1)\alpha\in(-1,1), and also the existence of Hölder continuous profile functions ω∈Cβ\omega\in C^{\beta} for all aa with some exponent α∈(−1,2​β−1)\alpha\in(-1,2\beta-1) and β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1). See also Zhen [Zhe23].

Chen et al. [CHH21] discovered the existence of compactly supported self-similar solutions to the De Gregorio model (a=1a=1) with the scaling exponent α=−2\alpha=-2. See also Huang et al. [HTW23].

Chen [Che20] and Lushikov et al. [LSS21] found the explicit solution for a=1/2a=1/2 with the scaling exponent α=2\alpha=2:

ω⁡(x)=−2​b​x(x2+b2)2,u⁡(x)=xx2+b2,b=38.\displaystyle\omega(x)=-\frac{2bx}{(x^{2}+b^{2})^{2}},\quad u(x)=\frac{x}{x^{2}+b^{2}},\quad b=\sqrt{\frac{3}{8}}.

Lushikov et al. [LSS21] numerically found the threshold ac≈0.689a_{c}\approx 0.689 for concentrating α>−1\alpha>-1 and expanding α<−1\alpha<-1 self-similarities. Huang et al. [HQWW24, Theorem 2.4] demonstrated the existence of solutions for all a≤1a\leq 1 with some exponent α⁡(a)∈[−2,2]\alpha(a)\in[-2,2]. The constructed solutions satisfy the asymptotic

ω⁡(x)=O⁡(1|x|α⁡(a)+1)as​|x|→∞,\displaystyle\omega(x)=O\left(\frac{1}{|x|^{\alpha(a)+1}}\right)\quad\textrm{as}\ |x|\to\infty,

for α⁡(a)>−1\alpha(a)>-1 and compact support for α⁡(a)<−1\alpha(a)<-1. The solutions [EJ20b], [Zhe23], [HTW23], and [HQWW24] are constructed via fixed-point theorems. Figure 5 summarizes the advection constant a≤1a\leq 1 and the scaling exponent α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R}.

A.2. Multi-dimensional shock singularities

A classic example of a nonlinear hyperbolic equation exhibiting a blow-up from smooth data is the 1D Burgers equation

ut+u​ux=0,x∈ℝ.\displaystyle u_{t}+uu_{x}=0,\quad x\in\mathbb{R}.

The self-similar equation

αα+1​u+1α+1​x​ux+u​ux=0,x∈ℝ,\displaystyle\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+1}u+\frac{1}{\alpha+1}xu_{x}+uu_{x}=0,\quad x\in\mathbb{R},

admits smooth solutions satisfying u⁡(x)=O⁡(|x|−α)u(x)=O(|x|^{-\alpha}) as |x|→∞|x|\to\infty for the scaling exponents

α=−12​i+1,i∈ℕ.\displaystyle\alpha=-\frac{1}{2i+1},\quad i\in\mathbb{N}.

See, e.g., [EF09]. The solution for α=−1/3\alpha=-1/3 [CSW96] forming

u1​(x)=(−x2−x24+127)13−(x2+x24+127)13,\displaystyle u_{1}(x)=\left(-\frac{x}{2}-\sqrt{\frac{x^{2}}{4}+\frac{1}{27}}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}-\left(\frac{x}{2}+\sqrt{\frac{x^{2}}{4}+\frac{1}{27}}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}},

is particularly important for the stability of blow-up solutions in the 11D Burgers equation [EF09] (This solution can be computed via the inverse equation x=−u−u−1/αx=-u-u^{-1/\alpha} by setting u=a1/3−b1/3u=a^{1/3}-b^{1/3} and solving the quadratic equation a−b=−xa-b=-x and a​b=1/27ab=1/27). Non-smooth solutions exist for non-integers i>0i>0 [CGM22].

Self-similar solutions depending on two variables involve an additional scaling exponent β∈ℝ\beta\in\mathbb{R}; see Table 1. The associated self-similar equations form

αα+1​u+1α+1​x​ux+βα+1​y​uy+u​ux=0,(x,y)∈ℝ2.\displaystyle\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+1}u+\frac{1}{\alpha+1}xu_{x}+\frac{\beta}{\alpha+1}yu_{y}+uu_{x}=0,\quad(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}.

Collot et al. [CGM22] found the solution for (α,β)=(−1/3,1/3)(\alpha,\beta)=(-1/3,1/3):

u⁡(x,y)=1F⁡(y)​u1​(F3/2​(y)​x),F⁡(y)=11+y2,\displaystyle u(x,y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{F(y)}}u_{1}(F^{3/2}(y)x),\quad F(y)=\frac{1}{1+y^{2}},

in the study of the Burgers equation with transverse viscosity ut+u​ux−uy​y=0u_{t}+uu_{x}-u_{yy}=0. More generally, the work [CGM22] found the solutions u(x,y)=Fk−1/2(y)u1(Fk3/2(y)x)u(x,y)=F_{k}^{-1/2}(y)u_{1}(F_{k}^{3/2}(y)x), Fk​(y)=(1+y2​k)−1F_{k}(y)=(1+y^{2k})^{-1} for (α,β)=(−1/3,1/(3k))(\alpha,\beta)=(-1/3,1/(3k)) and k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}.

Self-similar solutions depending on three variables involve two additional scaling exponents β,γ∈ℝ\beta,\gamma\in\mathbb{R} and the associated self-similar equations form

αα+1​u+1α+1​x​ux+βα+1​y​uy++γα+1​z​uz+u​ux=0,(x,y,z)∈ℝ3.\displaystyle\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+1}u+\frac{1}{\alpha+1}xu_{x}+\frac{\beta}{\alpha+1}yu_{y}++\frac{\gamma}{\alpha+1}zu_{z}+uu_{x}=0,\quad(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^{3}.

The function u(x,y,z)=F−1/2(r)u1(F3/2(r)x)u(x,y,z)=F^{-1/2}(r)u_{1}(F^{3/2}(r)x) for r=y2+z2r=\sqrt{y^{2}+z^{2}} is a solution to this equation for (α,β,γ)=(−1/3,1/3,1/3)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=(-1/3,1/3,1/3) [BSV23a, 2.7]. Buckmaster et al. [BSV23a, A.1] constructed a 1010D family of solutions to this equation for (α,β,γ)=(−1/3,1/3,1/3)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=(-1/3,1/3,1/3) by Taylor expansion and described shock formation of the 3D isentropic compressible Euler equations, cf. [BSV22], [BSV23b].

A.3. Two-dimensional separation singularities

The inviscid Prandtl equations model singularity formations of the Prandtl boundary layer equations:

ut+u​ux+v​uy\displaystyle u_{t}+uu_{x}+vu_{y} =0,\displaystyle=0,
ux+vy\displaystyle u_{x}+v_{y} =0,(x,y)∈ℝ2+,\displaystyle=0,\quad(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+},
v⁡(x,0,t)\displaystyle v(x,0,t) =0,x∈ℝ.\displaystyle=0,\quad x\in\mathbb{R}.

Self-similar solutions to these equations possess two scaling exponents α,β∈ℝ\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R} and the associated self-similar equation form

αα+1​u+1α+1​x​ux+βα+1​y​uy+u​ux+v​uy\displaystyle\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+1}u+\frac{1}{\alpha+1}xu_{x}+\frac{\beta}{\alpha+1}yu_{y}+uu_{x}+vu_{y} =0,\displaystyle=0,
ux+vy\displaystyle u_{x}+v_{y} =0,(x,y)∈ℝ+2,\displaystyle=0,\quad(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+},
v⁡(x,0)\displaystyle v(x,0) =0,x∈ℝ.\displaystyle=0,\quad x\in\mathbb{R}.

Collot et al. [CGM22, Lemma 3.1] found a new way to solve this equation for α≠0\alpha\neq 0 using a volume-preserving Crocco transform. Namely, (u,v)(u,v) solves the self-similar equation if and only if there exists a function b⁡(x,y)b(x,y) such that the mapping (x,y)⟼(a,b)(x,y)\longmapsto(a,b) for a⁡(x,y)=−u⁡(x,y)a(x,y)=-u(x,y) is a volume-preserving diffeomorphism and the inverse function x=x⁡(a,b)x=x(a,b) solves the equation

−αα+1​a​xa+β−α+1α+1​b​xb=1α+1​x−a.\displaystyle-\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+1}ax_{a}+\frac{\beta-\alpha+1}{\alpha+1}bx_{b}=\frac{1}{\alpha+1}x-a.

The work [CGM22, Lemma 3.1] found two explicit solutions for α=−1/3\alpha=-1/3:

x=a+b2+C​a3,β=−16,\displaystyle x=a+b^{2}+Ca^{3},\quad\beta=-\frac{1}{6},
x=a+a3+14​a​b2,β=−13.\displaystyle x=a+a^{3}+\frac{1}{4}ab^{2},\quad\beta=-\frac{1}{3}.

The case β=−1/6\beta=-1/6 is a generic boundary layer separation singularity relevant to Van-Dommelen–Shen singularity, and the case β=−1/3\beta=-1/3 is a degenerate singularity relevant to Burgers shock; see [CGIM22] for a stability result in the Prandtl boundary layer equations.

and α=αn\alpha=\alpha_{n} admits a smooth spherically symmetric profile function (u,ρ)(u,\rho) satisfying

u⁡(x)=O⁡(1|x|αα+1),ρ⁡(x)=O⁡(1|x|2​αα+1)as​|x|→∞.\displaystyle u(x)=O\left(\frac{1}{|x|^{\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+1}}}\right),\quad\rho(x)=O\left(\frac{1}{|x|^{\frac{2\alpha}{\alpha+1}}}\right)\quad\textrm{as}\ |x|\to\infty.

The mass of this density ρ\rho is infinite. Buckmaster et al. [BCLGSa] demonstrated the existence of smooth spherically symmetric solutions for all adiabatic exponent γ>1\gamma>1 by studying phase portraits associated with Riemann invariants; see [BCLGSb] for a review.
